chapter: Hines 1935-38, Gus Arnheim and Billy Eckstine
title: Fort Lauderdale 1938: segregated laws and armed musicians
summary: Hinton asks for the Earl Hines story; police keep white women away from the bandstand and the band carries guns.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I think we better wind this up. I'd like to wind this up just by doing some rehashing and going over some of the things that we've been talking about. This one story, I think we can digress here a little bit, because there was a beautiful story that I think you intended to tell me about Earl Hines.
When you were working -- you can just name the year and what happened. Go right ahead.

Okay. Well, this was the year of 1938, before the -- that we split the Earl Hines band up, you know. We were on tour, and we went to Fort Lauderdale, Florida. Well, back there it wasn't too cool -- I mean, they had laws down there. For instance, there were some New York white musicians who came to see us before, you know, when we pulled up the bus to go in and say hello, and everything. And the cops came up there and stopped us from talking to each other.

And it was like against the law, really. So anyway, we went into this bar room in Fort Lauderdale, and we started to play. Now they had 15 state troopers there just to keep down any confusion, you know, because here's some Black cats. We're playing in this white place, and they kept all the white women away from the bandstand, wouldn't
let them talk to us. They couldn't even come up and make a request, so the men --

Well, we had a big band. I think we had about 17 pieces. Let's see -- five reeds, eight brass, 13, four full rhythm, 17 pieces. And -- well, the band was so big until all of us couldn't get on the bandstand. All could get on the bandstand but Earl. The bandstand must have stood about -- off the floor -- maybe four or five feet. And then right on the floor next to the bandstand they put the piano for Earl to play, so he was down on the floor.

We were like looking down on him, and at that time all of us carried guns because we had a kind of wild man. A cat say, well, I got to go. Somebody's going to mess with me. I mean, I'm not just going to let him slap me on both cheeks and knock me down, drag me out and lynch me without a fight. That was our attitude. You know, things were very bad.
